#4215. Xbox Series S Trashed By Tekken Director Ketsuhiro Harada

A senior Xbox official and former Tekken director Katsuhiro Harada walk into a bar. Harada whips up a Dragon Uppercut, but the Xbox official tells him the Series S can't handle that many projectiles on screen.

Harada isn't exactly shy when it comes to saying what's on his mind, so when he actually did walk into a room with an Xbox official at the Console Game Developers Conference 2026 in South Korea, he took the opportunity to tear into the Series S then and there—worrying that other devs being overly polite might give Microsoft the idea to do it again with Project Helix.

"There's something I really want to say while I have the floor," Harada said (translated by Inven Global). "Since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released."

The panel, moderated by former Sony president Shuhei Yoshida, also featured Shift Up CTO DongKi Lee, Too Kyo Games CEO Kazutaka Kodaka, CD Projekt Red associate game director Paweł Sasko, and Ludeon Studios CEO Tynan Sylvester. Harada appeared as the CEO of the newly formed VS Studio, and after making it clear he wasn't a fan of the Series S, he turned to his peers and asked Sasko whether he was "upset inside" because of it.

Sasko "burst out laughing" before saying, "It constantly throws challenges at us and forces us to optimize our code very cleanly."

Harada doubled down, "You just used a very polite and elegant way to say, 'Xbox Series S sucks,' right? Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance. When porting to Switch 2, developers can shift their mindset to 'Switch 2 is a distinct device for Nintendo fans!' But with Xbox, after delivering your absolute best output, it feels like having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child."

Director Paweł packaged Series S so gracefully that the Microsoft representative in the audience keeps nodding along. I'm worried they'll feel reassured and release a successor like 'Helix S' for the next-gen Xbox as well.

He isn't the only dev to run into a brick wall with the Xbox Series S, either. Baldur's Gate 3 was infamously delayed on Xbox because Larian Studios couldn't ensure parity between the two consoles, struggling to get split-screen co-op working on the Series S (though the studio assured it isn't holding back next-gen). Bossa Studios VFX artist Ian Maclure also claimed in 2022 that "MANY developers have been sitting in meetings for the past year desperately trying to get Series S launch requirements dropped," describing it as "an albatross around the neck of production." A sentiment echoed by Digital Foundry's Alexander Battagalia, who reported that several developers find the memory constraints frustrating.

But there's another issue with the Series S that's less talked about, which Harada takes issue with. "Furthermore, in markets like the US, there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners," he explained. "Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking 'Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?'"

Asha Sharma wants Xbox to be an attractive partner for developers and creatives, despite being poised to lay off a bunch of developers and creatives.

The Xbox Series S was offered up as the 'budget' next-gen console, so it's understandable that developers like Harada are frustrated when those buying the cheaper alternative get angry over their games looking, well, cheaper. There have been murmurs for years that studios are fed up with having to accommodate two different Xbox consoles, but we don't know enough about how Project Helix will work yet to say whether Microsoft will address those concerns.

"I personally think Dark Souls has fairly simple action mechanics, and I don’t actually consider it to be an especially difficult game."

#4214. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) Review - Exceptionally Familiar

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is the most important video game ever made… to me. My byline would not appear in the pages of Game Informer without my original experience playing that game. But it is nearly 30 years old, and despite establishing many important staples of 3D gaming, its age is becoming more apparent. Ocarina of Time was due for a re-examination, and its remake is a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element: visuals, storytelling, timeless design, and more. It is, however, a remake, and the coloring (though expertly done) is firmly inside the lines.

Ocarina of Time is gorgeous. That the game is less than 25 GB is an engineering marvel. I never quite came around to the odd looks of child Link or Zelda, but every other character, environment, enemy, item, and boss looks incredible. I eagerly looked forward to meeting every weirdo in Hyrule to see their new look, and was never disappointed. The ReDeads and Stalchildren are more traumatic than ever, and every NPC childhood crush I thought I had moved on from was reignited. Watching the sun rise and set over Hyrule feels as magical as it did in the past.

The same accolades can be awarded to the soundtrack. The new orchestrations are incredible, and watching Link’s 4K fingers play the proper notes on his ocarina is mesmerizing. Nintendo continues to fumble voice acting with stiff performances, but thankfully the vast majority of dialogue – one of the primary changes in this remake – is not spoken. Characters don’t necessarily have more to say, but what they say is more impactful, and there are a handful of small but exciting expansions to character and story details. Nothing is groundbreaking or changes how you look at familiar elements, but it manages to be simultaneously nostalgic and improved.

And that’s the closest I got to what I would debatably call a problem: It all looks new, but doesn’t feel particularly new. Ocarina’s overall design holds up. The time travel element is surprising and creates great opportunities to see the world change and evolve; puzzles and their solutions are rewarding; the basics of combat, though simple, are thrilling. All those elements have been adjusted, but not overhauled. Dungeons and their puzzles have been tweaked to remove annoyances (such as fewer keys in the Water Temple), and the new swordplay effects make connecting your blade to monsters feel incredible. But they’re all ultimately small changes that don’t cast Ocarina in a new light or consider its history. It’s a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it in this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

The beautiful 2026 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time does not study the legacy or impact of the landmark game on the video game medium. Instead, it is a meticulous and incredibly impressive recreation of one of the best games ever made. I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry. For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game again 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve that original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn’t expect to be so moved.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

#4213. New Discord Setting Will Let You Take Over Streamed Games

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

The battle of online chat platforms used to be very close, with a wide range of selections that friends all had to choose between before getting started. Nowadays, the vast majority of gamers are centralized on one platform, allowing that platform to keep them engaged with constant small iterations and improvements.

Deadlock is starting to suffer from the same fate as other free-to-play games, with bot farmers crawling from the woodwork.

Of course, that platform is Discord, an online group chat and voice call app that seems like it's always adding new bells and whistles. Recently leaked, Discord is apparently working on a new function that will allow viewers of a friend’s stream to ask them to “pass the controller”, handing over direct control of the game being played to whoever has requested it.

As magical as this system may sound, it actually isn’t all that far-fetched, serving as a major selling point for the app Parsec, which specializes in allowing players to connect to each other's PCs, allowing online play of typically local-only titles. Steam’s Steamplay system functions similarly, though it requires players to provide their own feed of the game.

Discord’s offering of the function could be a major game changer, consolidating multiple functions into an already centralized app. The issue of latency and ping will always exist, but the company is doing a lot to earn back the users who were shaken by their recent collaboration with Google to open up channel messages directly to searches.

Aimed at opening up servers that exist to share info and house massive communities, no real hiccups have occurred yet, even as users stay vigilant. Discord has utilized all kinds of different minigames and in-app connections to keep users centralized on the app itself, to a fairly mixed effect.

The inclusion of the token shop and various quests to allow users to obtain cosmetics and even Nitro time for free was a massive success, allowing Discord to basically incentivize users to sit through various ads and sponsored quests. Discord has made it clear they aim to turn the app into more than just a chat venue.

Nowadays, the vast majority of gamers are centralized on one platform, allowing that platform to keep them engaged with constant small iterations and improvements.

This function has yet to be formally announced, and hasn’t had any kind of estimated release date presented, but could seriously enable a lot of older co-op games that don’t have modern releases or online multiplayer. Alongside the huge amount of game preservation work that takes place inside of Discord servers, this is potentially one of Discord’s most impactful updates, for better or for worse.

The only issue that may creep up on Discord is the eternal hex of feature creep, the mixtape where developers focus on implementing more things instead of fixing and finalizing the things they have now. Discord has really focused on adding more, with some real dust appearing on basic functions like voice calls. Latency has been increasing, and it takes longer to join on average.

These issues are annoying, but nothing overly serious, at least for now. The worry is always that functions like this, that allow players to control input on other users' machines, could be maliciously abused one way or another, either through modifications or exploitable bugs.

This is the same type of worry that users had about the Google initiative, and while nothing has come of it yet, users find it safer to err on the side of caution. Discord’s history of data breaches is far from spotless, and this kind of direct access could lead to real abuse if not properly put together. The function is likely to roll out slowly through some form of beta, but until official word is out, all we can do is speculate.

#4212. Nioh 3 is, unsurprisingly, the fastest-selling game in the series with over a million units sold

Nioh 3 has taken the Nioh franchise to new heights, delivering its biggest-ever launch.

Even before the game came out, it was pretty easy to guess that Nioh 3 would be a hit. From the word of mouth leading up to launch, to the well-received free demo, there was little chance the action RPG wasn’t going to be a major deal.

Today, publisher Koei Tecmo has announced that the game has officially passed over one million copies sold worldwide across PC, and PlayStation 5. This makes it the fastest in the Nioh franchise to reach this milestone.

As a result of this fantastic launch, Nioh 3 has now pushed overall Nioh franchise sales to be over 10 million, which includes the original Nioh as well as Nioh 2. Today’s news comes just two weeks after the game arrived on PC, and PS5.

On Steam, where it’s available on PC, it shot up the Steam charts, and immediately broke the series’ previous best peak concurrent player count record. From there, the numbers kept growing, leading up to a stellar weekend where it peaked at 88,045 concurrent players on Steam, double that of its launch day.

This now stands as the largest for any Nioh game on Steam, and though we don’t have insight into how well it’s doing on PS5 specifically, it still shows that the Nioh series continues to grow.

Nioh 3 builds on everything the two prior games established, and pushes the series into the semi-open-world realm, with several larger maps that each cover a period of time in Japan’s history. In our Nioh 3 review we called it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.”

#4209. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.

#4208. Gallery: Hollow Knight & Silksong's Switch 2 Physicals Are A Delight For Map Fans

Fangamer announced earlier this year that it had two swanky new Switch 2 physical releases in the works for both Hollow Knight and Silksong, each complete with a couple of bonus goodies inside the box.

With the release date finally upon us, the good folks over at Fangamer have sent us a copy of each, and let it be known, they are both really rather sexy.

Both boxes boast wrap-around cover art (for some particularly detailed spines) and reversible sleeves so you can opt for a design without all of the Switch 2 T&C text down at the bottom.

All of the DLC for the first game is included on the cart, too, and while Silksong's Sea of Sorrow expansion obviously isn't on there at the moment (we're still waiting for a firm release date on that one), it will come as a free download to all those with a copy when it eventually drops.

Inside, both copies contain some bonus booklet goodies, too. Each has its own instruction booklet, containing introductions for everything from both the Knight and Hornet's movesets and upgrade abilities, to points of interest in the world. Gosh, we didn't realise how much we had missed physical manuals.

A physical copy of each game's map is included in the box as well, which folds up into a little wax-stamped envelope — a very neat touch, if we've ever seen one. This gives you a detailed rundown of each location for both games, and could prove as a valuable route tracker for those still trying to uncover Hallownest/Pharloom's secrets.

Both the Hollow Knight and Silksong Switch 2 physicals are now available on the Fangamer website.

#4207. God Of War Laufey Delayed To May

PlayStation first-party developer Santa Monica Studio has delayed its upcoming action game, God of War Laufey, to May. More specifically, the PlayStation 5-exclusive title will now launch on May 20, representing a roughly three-month delay from the original February 16 release date.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen," a statement from the studio reads. "We don't take for granted the trusted place in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans. With this in mind, we've made the decision to delay God of War Laufey's release to May 20, 2027. We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon."

God of War Laufey stars Faye, Kratos' deceased wife from his Norse adventures, after she ends up in the mysterious realm known as the Everywhen following her death. There, she will fight monsters and creatures from various mythologies alongside a talking gelatinous cube and a talking sword sash. We'll have to wait a bit longer than expected now to see what her adventure entails.

God of War Laufey will now launch on PS5 next year on May 20. In the meantime, check out this newly revealed weapon, then read about how Amazon's God of War TV series has recast Kratos as Dave Bautista.

#4205. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

#4204. Zelda Ocarina Remake Producers Talk Changing And Maintaining The Game, Easter Eggs, The Bombchu Bowling Alley Operator, And More

Today marks the release of the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2. You can read my full, positive review here. Ahead of the game’s release, but after having played the game to completion (well… 99% as you will learn below), I traveled to New York to speak with Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma (whose work on the original Ocarina of Time marked his first involvement with the series) and Ocarina of Time remake producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi (director of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom among other Zelda titles).

Topics include how the team approached remaking Ocarina of Time, what needed changing and what needed to stay the same, their thoughts on the Easter Eggs from the original game, the fate and marital status of the Bombchu Bowling girl, and more.

The discussion covers a fairly faithful remake of Ocarina of Time for Nintendo 64, which launched nearly 30 years ago, but I have spoiler-marked certain questions and answers that might be considered sensitive if you want to maintain surprise when playing the remake yourself.

Mr. Fujibayashi, what is your relationship to Ocarina of Time?

Fujibayashi: Regarding the original Ocarina of Time, at the time I was working for a different company, so it was mainly me as an end user trying to looking forward to the experience of what a 3D Zelda is going to look like. So, really, I was just waiting in anticipation for that.

How long has the remake been in development?

Aonuma: It's actually kind of hard to say exactly when development began because the earliest thought process was us thinking about the 40th anniversary of The Legend of Zelda approaching, and so we started to have this conversation, “Oh, what should we make to mark this occasion?” And then at that point, we decided on Ocarina of Time, and so a lot of time elapsed from the beginning of that conversation about the anniversary until we got to Ocarina. So it's hard to pinpoint exactly when the development itself began.

Was this a more relaxing game to develop after making Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom back-to-back?

Aonuma: Was it relaxing? That's kind of a hard question to ask. I would say it's more a different style of development. So, if we looked at Tears of the Kingdom, Breath of the Wild, these were created as new games with a very different kind of development cycle. Whereas for a remake like this one, we decided to take an interesting approach, which is to bring in this new younger staff and find out what they would bring to this project in terms of their own experience, their own interpretation as newer staff.

And so my role here was really advising them on this, and it's not always like the development cycle of a new game. But in one sense, the producer has to be careful not to advise too much, to say that you must do it like this. You don't want to prescribe the approach that anyone is going to take. You want to make sure that there's enough space for these younger staff members to have their own interpretation, their own approach to it.

Do you have remake philosophies or rules, like what needs to stay the same and what should change?

Fujibayashi: So, in fact, there were pretty clear kind of rules or guidelines, as you said. First, is because you know, as Mr. Aonuma had mentioned, where he wanted to, the development team was centered around the young directors that took part in this development. And when we first started discussing what kind of game and what kind of approach you wanted to take. One thing that really came through and we clarified was, as you mentioned, what are we going to change and what are we going to keep the same.

And I'll start with what we wanted to change, and that was really to make sure that – because we have the ability to use the latest technology through the Nintendo Switch 2 – there's a lot we can change and improve upon, such as you know obviously things like controls, graphics. We also have a new controller, so that allows for the new camera controls. And we’re really able to fine tune and polish the feel of the game and there was excitement for all the ways of expression we can provide the player.

But on the other hand, thinking about what we didn't want to change, we were thinking about the creators of the original Ocarina of Time, and what they wanted to convey, the experience that they wanted to provide for users and players through this title. That's something that we wanted to keep intact and that spirit to carry across. And we wanted to make sure that this new game is able to deliver that in the way that we wanted them to.

Aonuma: So speaking as someone who worked on the original Ocarina of Time for Nintendo 64, you always have those moments looking back of, “Oh, you know, I really wanted to do more of this,” or, “I wanted to be able to express this in a different way,” but you're faced with certainly the tech limitations of the time. And I went on from Ocarina of Time to work on other Zelda franchise titles, as well. And with each new title, you're always looking for a new way to express something that may not have been available to you previously. But you always have to keep in mind is what makes a Zelda game special, and how do we protect that? How do we keep that in store for the players, as well. So, on this project in particular, I had to think of that through the lens of how do we protect the things that make it the Zelda Ocarina experience, but also how do I give the freedom to the staff to find their own expression of these ideas? And I think between those two things, we found a really good balance. So I'm very happy about that.

When we interviewed you, Mr. Aonuma, for Game Informer’s Breath of the Wild cover story, Shigeru Miyamoto was present, and he made a joke about the challenge of the water temple. Are you happy with where the Water Temple is now in the remake?

Aonuma: Certainly, looking back on the challenge level of the Water Temple, I think it was hard, but some of that came from the system that we were presenting to players. So, for example, if you look at the way that players used to have to switch to the heavy iron boots so that they could sink in the water, you had to go to a different screen and press the button. But now that we're able to give players a shortcut, single button on the gameplay screen, I think they can get to that more quickly. It's a better experience because they can focus on solving the puzzle rather than having to navigate menus and thinking about that and interrupting the flow of their thought each time.

Another consideration compared to the original is that you couldn't move the camera angle in the original game, and so if you were looking for a certain room in this 3D space relative to where you are now, it was much more difficult to orient yourself and think about the space where that room might exist. So I think those two together, you know, also with the heavy boots being one button press, I think this, for me, is the best version of the Water Temple.

Is the canon of the Zelda timeline considered at all during development? Did you think about adding in Easter eggs that made references to things that would have happened later in the Zelda story? Like Wind Waker taking place after Ocarina of Time, for example.

Aonuma: It's funny because the staff would sometimes ask me about the possibility of including nods to the timeline or references to the other game, and I actually, at the time, would say, "No, let's focus on this game. Let's make this the best version of Ocarina of Time that we can." So, the timeline was in the back of our mind, but we didn't consider taking an approach to this game where we actually, explicitly included references like that.

When testing the game, was it challenging to find people who had never played Ocarina of Time?

Aonuma: As it turns out, both on our staff and in the testing teams, there's a lot of young people, and many of them had never played the original. So it wasn't a challenge to find them.

Who do you primarily consider this remake to be for? New people who have never played Ocarina? Or fans like myself who consider it to be, frankly, their favorite game. Who is the important audience?

Fujibayashi: The answer is both. Our response to those fans who have fond memories of this title is really what I mentioned earlier: being able to provide the experience of what it was like to play Ocarina of Time back to them, and that was our response to them. And when it comes to the players that are experiencing this for the first time, whether it's the graphics, or the controls, or the ability to shift and move the camera; those are all changes and fine-tuning that we've made to make sure that people who are used to modern gaming are able to enter this experience with as little friction as possible. So again, to answer your question? It's really both.

Aonuma: Certainly, when you look at the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, there is so much hidden in the world that people spend a lot of time looking for things. And your first time playing through, you may not find all of it in one go. People in that kind of situation would refer to strategy books and information that they can find.

For example, when you're looking for the like last Skulltala and you already have 99, our job is to think about how to give the player an approach to that sort of a problem. What kind of information can we give them to help out. To make it a fun, but still challenging experience, because we want even new players to come in and to be able to fully experience this world that we've created for them, even though old fans are going to come in with a little bit of an advantage in the form of a lot of prior game knowledge.

I'm not kidding about needing some help with that final Skulltala. I'm going to hand you my Switch 2 after this so you can show me where it is because it's been driving me crazy. I've been having dreams about where the final Skulltala might be.

The end of the game in the remake made me emotional in a way I wasn't expecting. It made me cry, just the whole ending of the experience overall. Were you expecting that kind of reaction from players?

Fujibayashi: So first, I want to say I'm very, very happy and excited to hear you say that because, as you mentioned, that cutscene – cutscenes in general – but that cutscene specifically is something that we, as a dev team, heavily discussed. Because of the limitations of the technology back in the day, there might have been things that we weren't able to convey fully, whether it's because of the tempo of the game… whatever it is. And so, when we approached this remake, we wanted to make sure that we captured that moment in the way that we wanted to express it. So that the right kinds of emotions are evoked, and that we can convey the emotion and the story that we wanted to at that moment. And now that hearing you say that and kind of having that reaction really struck a chord? I'm really relieved to hear that because that's exactly what we wanted to do.

The ReDeads, the Shadow Temple, the Dead Hand miniboss, Wall Masters – these enemies traumatized a whole generation of kids. I'm curious if that was always the intention and how did you approach making sure that those elements still remained scary? Was there a line that was too scary?

Aonuma: Certainly, at the time, we had this intent to make sure that we allow the players to find the enemies a little bit scary. They have to be, right? We want to express that sort of thing. But more than anything, they are part of this Fantasy world, which has both light and dark portions, and so we're trying to bring that feeling across. It’s not that we're trying to scare people outright as the entire intent, but rather show that you know Link is part of a brighter part of the world where people are friendly, and Ganon is a part of the darker part of the world where there's a lot of scary things. And we kept that in mind in the remake as well.

We wanted to make sure we were bringing that out, but the tools that we have available to us now for expression are so capable that if we really tried, of course, we could make something that was very, very scary. But this is supposed to be for all kinds of players. We didn't want to hit the scary notes so strongly that we were putting off new players or younger players, and so we want to have that tuning very carefully in mind as we're making those adjustments in terms of presenting that final expression in the game.

I shudder to visualize what the scarier versions of the ReDeads might look like.

Aonuma: What was your experience of them this time?

Oh, terrifying! That noise. The noise they make. That scream. I feel it in my chest. It just recalls that scariness of my childhood in a way that I admit is very entertaining, and I like. Do you remember recording that sound effect? How did you do that? Did you have someone scream?

For the remake, a lot has been rewritten. The meaning hasn't been changed dramatically, but pretty much everything has been rewritten. What was the goal with the rewriting overall?

Fujibayashi: Yes, it's as you said. We did a lot of rewriting of the text. When it comes to the original Ocarina of Time, there's the idea that because it was 28 years ago – it's a long time ago – there's the turn of phrase, or the way it's been written, is sometimes not clear or doesn't work in the modern day, given the context of the modern day. And so that's why we wanted to make sure that it makes sense and it's easier to understand for people who are familiar with playing modern games, and also that it works better here.

And when you think about… obviously the graphics have been improved significantly. Before we had to do things like… “That blue ocarina that is the size that you could fit on a hand,” something like that, to make sure that the idea gets across to the player. But now, because the graphics are improved, it's very clear what the size it is. It's very clear that it's a blue ocarina. So with the new graphics, if you go through the wordy explanation of what it is, the player is going to be like, "Yeah, I can see it." So in order to make sure that we remove those kind of slight hurdles and really make sure that we can present the game and improve not only the expression but also the pacing of the game? That's something that we really took into consideration as we were rewriting the game.

I wanted to ask about some specific changes for the remake. You get five bottles now. Why?

Aonuma: Because bottles are so important to the way the player plays the game, like looking for strategies to deal with different kinds of situations, even at the time of development of the original title, I thought, “Oh, you know, I could do with even just one more bottle.” I think certainly when you collect all four in the original, you feel great about that at time. But I was still thinking like one more would be okay, right?

So, all this time that was in the back of my mind. But when the new younger staff were familiarizing themselves with the old game and thinking about what they might want to change in this version, one thing that I suggested was that the player could get their first bottle earlier, and this would actually be really useful in terms of reinforcing for the player how helpful bottles were and motivating them on their quest to find the next bottle. It strengthens that whole sequence through the game by changing the order just a little bit there. But yeah, certainly, once you have a certain number of bottles, you're going to feel a little bit more confident and more comfortable. But reinforcing that feeling early on, I think, was important for us in the development of this one.

In the original, there were Nintendo character portraits in Zelda's courtyard of Mario, Yoshi, and more, but those have been removed. I was curious as to why.

Aonuma: Certainly, at the time, when we put those there, I don't think anybody thought it was too big a deal. Maybe there was a more carefree or comfortable approach to that sort of thing. But looking at it now, like if a player is coming through that area, and given the overall way that we're, you know, creating this world and giving the player that form of expression, if they look up and they think, "Why is Yoshi there?” We don't want that moment to interrupt their experience of the world in that way. So we're feeling a little bit differently about it this time.

However, you will remember that there is one design element on Talon with Bowser on it, and that's part of the original design of the character. So we didn't change that. That stays as is.

I have some short-answer questions. The woman who runs the Bombchu Bowling game. What happened to her after seven years. And is she single?

Aonuma: That's something we're not going to touch, and I'll leave it to your imagination.

One of the Skulltala rewards is Bombchus, which I found disappointing when I was young, and I found disappointing as an adult. Why does he give you Bombchus?

Aonuma: So that feeling you had when you got, as a reward for a certain number of Skulltalas, the Bombchus, and you thought, “Wait, that's it?” That's also part of the original experience of the 64 version. So there, there's an approach that we take where we try to keep all of the different notes that people felt in the original game in place. You know, sometimes it's really remarkable, fun things, and other times it's slight moments of disappointment. Even that could be memorable in that way. It's important to maintain that.

The Great Fairies. What do they need rupees for?

Fujibayashi: You know, it's really about a feeling. It's like in Japan sometimes, like donations to a temple or something similar like that. It's to express your reverence for the great fairies.

The 3DS remake had Skyward Sword art hidden in a couple of places, but you removed it for this remake. You didn't want to keep the Skyward Sword art?

Aonuma: [Laughs] I do remember at the time the designers on the 3DS version were really interested in placing Easter Eggs like that throughout the game, and the timing of the release of Skyward Sword was such that it was perfect to go ahead and include that. So I said, “Okay, sure.” But like earlier when we were talking about in the courtyard sequence with the Yoshi portrait. You know, you don't want to interrupt the player's experience by seeing something that's unrelated to what they're currently doing in the game. So for that reason, we decided not to go that way.

Mr. Fujibayashi, you directed Skyward Sword. Were you sad to see that reference removed?

Fujibayashi: [Laughs] No, it’s really as Mr. Aonuma said. There was an underlying concept in what we were going for, so no hard feelings there.

I think the biggest cutscene change in the game is when Link transitions from child to adult. It is now a much more involved sequence. Why did that scene need such a drastic change?

Aonuma: So I think that's really connected to the way we were thinking about expressing things in the original. We couldn't do everything. We couldn't express everything that we'd like to, and I think in that moment where you have Ganondorf having this reaction to Link becoming older, that cutscene in the original, it was very low on explanation.

So, you have these thoughts in the player's mind like, “Oh wait, why is he there? What's the relation to this process?” So, you want something that explains his presence, that explains his reaction to make a bigger impression on the player overall, and that's something that you can use to connect the motivation to want to face Ganondorf in the final fight. Something that I think comes across better now.

[I pulled out my Switch 2 and showed them how I was missing one Skulltala in Hyrule Field]

You can see here I have 99 out of 100 and am have two out of three in Hyrule Field. Can you point to a general location to give me an idea of where to look?

For Game Informer's review of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) follow the link.

#4203. Talking Point: With Big Walk, The AI-In-Game-Dev Debate Just Got A Lot Murkier

"The line must be drawn here! This far, no further!"

Please forgive the Captain Picard First Contact quote (it's been a couple of weeks since Patrick Stewart's death and only now can I mention his most famous character without welling up) - I promise it's relevant as an illustration of an admirable, principled stance.

In the Borg, good ol' Jean-Luc had a well-defined enemy to engage, with the threat of humanity's assimilation providing a pretty clear line between good and bad. There are larger philosophical questions about the hive mind and our aversion to Star Trek's cube-riding automatons, but for the purposes of this article, let's assume we're all in agreement: Borg=baaad.

Back in the real world, though, that line between right and wrong often isn't so easy to define. Today there'll be a lot of commentators in the video game space, players and developers alike, longing for a better understanding of another encroaching, all-consuming entity.

House House's belated disclosure that LLMs were used during the development of indie hit Big Walk pours fuel on an already raging debate and brings questions over permissible AI use in game dev right back into the discourse - specifically the differences between generative AI for player-facing audio-visual assets and writing versus coding and other less obvious uses.

News Big Walk Devs Issue Statement Over AI Usage

This latest flashpoint followed a statement released by a subset of IGF Award jurors explaining why they won't be voting for games developed using any form of generative AI.

Last year, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — which swept The Game Awards with nine wins from 13 nominations — raised similar questions after the Indie Game Awards disqualified Sandfall Interactive's game upon discovering AI had been used in the development pipeline.

I've voiced my distaste for GenAI, and it remains a massive no-no - professionally and personally. I'm fortunate to not have corporate overlords mandating its use around these parts, which certainly isn't the case for some other outlets, nor for many creatives in the gaming space. The gulf in quality between the human-written word and generated bilge is still enormous and easily identifiable, and for now, the same is broadly true of GenAI visual artwork, too.

What this Big Walk situation highlights, however, is how difficult it can be to discern in other places, and the increasing pull it has on even the most principled developers.

Talking Point Does It Bother You That Big Games Companies Are Using GenAI?

The phrase gets bandied around a lot, but it's fair to call Big Walk a proper 'critical darling'. It garnered "Universal Acclaim" back in August, with an impressive 91 Metascore. Alex gave it a "Great" 8/10 after reviewing the Switch 2 version for us - technical hiccups took the shine off it for him, but he still loved the co-op experience. And by September it was already Nile's GOTY.

As someone who didn't play Big Walk at launch, its place in my GOTY-catch-up priorities may have shifted, but wherever you land on the GenAI spectrum, the consensus among critics and players is as unanimous as it gets: Big Walk is an excellent video game.

There are many issues to consider — not least where AI use crosses from tool to theft — but an important one relates to how this game in particular has had a profound effect on many players. Rejecting something flagged as 'suspicious' on principle is easy, especially with so many brilliant games releasing each week. But something you've played already and internalised and loved? From a dev team you respect?

For some, this revelation will feel like when a beloved artist/actor/writer/musician is revealed to be problematic, but we're not talking about illegal behaviour or allegations here.

If House House's statement is to be taken at face value, the team used a chatbot to find a solution to a coding issue with Unity, the third-party engine the game is built on. People online with real chops have already investigated the specifics of House House's single example:

took me 3 hours but I figured out the “URP culling shadowcasters behind the camera” issue House House cites in their disclosure. This culls immediately when the object is off-camera, but modifying the culling params with a custom frustrum is straightforward

this needs cleaning up but is basically the gist

This was a terrible use of 3 hours, but I know just a bit more about how to do something cool. I’m sympathetic to them wanting to ship something good but AI rots your damn brain

That's the one example the devs offer in their statement, and the language around further usage feels vague. The impression it gives is of a team searching for a solution to a specific problem using common tools, as opposed to vibe-coding huge swathes of the game.

Now, I've never programmed anything in my life, but I can appreciate that efficient code must be an art in itself. Is it any less of an art because that code is invisible to players? Then again, to me, generating great chunks of game code feels very different from using an LLM to squash a bug or find a solution when third-party documentation fails. Is one usage as 'bad' as the other, or is this slippery slope, gateway-drug territory?

(Perhaps if any programmers are reading, they'd like to share thoughts in the comments - as the headline says, this is very much a talking point and I'm keen to explore with as much nuance as the internet will permit.)

My point is that seeing exactly where to draw that line is increasingly difficult when AI tools of all types become ubiquitous. A blanket rejection of anything inevitably now means excluding not just an increasing number of games, but also artistically significant, important ones.

And with executives like former Nintendo of America president Doug Bowser advocating the use of AI for indie teams to improve workflow, it's also easy to understand how a developer might turn to the tech. The whole topic is getting greyer by the day, much to the pleasure of evangelists, I'm sure.

Like it or not, this situation forces AI sceptics to reconcile their positive feelings for the game. House House estimates "well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code" has any trace of generative AI, but to paraphrase a certain Starfleet captain again, "How much does it take before it becomes wrong, hmm?" That is the question.

For some players who simply don't care, it's a non-issue. Some may reluctantly cut the game from their lives and GOTY lists. I suspect that others, though, disappointed or otherwise, will start reconsidering where they personally draw the AI line.

And if House House hadn't disclosed this, would anyone have ever known? I'd guess not. And if a celebrated indie team turned to AI as a problem-solver, how many other devs aren't disclosing similar usage? And how many sure-as-hell won't do so after this?

Lots of questions, no clear answers, just murk. How unsatisfying. I've heard 'ends-justify-means' sentiments online — 'hey, if the game is good, does it matter?' — which feel unsavoury given the documented, quantifiable damage AI is doing to the games industry and the wider world. It's that damage which has IGF jurors abstaining from voting for Big Walk this year: an understandable, admirable stance.

Which leads us to one final question: What would Captain Picard do?

Naturally, he'd call everyone into the Observation Lounge for a big old meeting in a calm, civilised manner, that's what. Conference.

Let us know below if this revelation changes your relationship with the game or where you draw the line when it comes to generative AI in its various forms.

"We deeply apologize for causing distrust"

News 'Everything Will Be Made by Humans': Expedition 33 Dev Says No More AI After Post-Awards Heat

Review Big Walk (Switch 2) - A Co-Op Adventure Like Nothing Else That Somehow Struggles On Switch 2

Gavin first wrote for Nintendo Life in 2018 before joining the site full-time the following year, rising through the ranks to become Editor. He can currently be found squashed beneath a Switch backlog the size of Normandy.

We are at the point where the townspeople grab their torches and pitchforks at any company who admits they used AI.

Look at the Dior Xmas commercial for instance, it doesn't matter what reasons or excuses are given, most are done listening.

Oh, gosh. That brainrot meme stuffs just the most idiotic thing ever. AI is just cancer. It doesn't even helping at all.

AI is destroying the planet and ruining drinkable water in the communities around data centers. If you're defending even the smallest use you're rolling over and exposing your bellies for the billionaires that ransack our planet for profit that are benefitting the most by it's use.

First off, I love that you quoted my favorite line from my favorite Trek film. Also thank you for bringing a nuanced approach to the issue while acknowledging you're general anti-AI attitude. I'll contribute my two cents on the issue.

I'm anti-AI in almost all facets of life, but I also have always said that no absolute is ever going to be proper (including that one). I see this particular instance as a very slippery slope. If it truly was nothing more than "We can't get this one thing to work like it should, and the entire team has spent hours trying to figure it out," then I can at least understand it. I'm very on the fence with it myself, but I'm leaning slightly to the "acceptable use" side with an asterisk of "It's always better to use purely human work, and this is the lazy way out." Again, just my opinion.

As for the inevitability of AI's spread in game development, I take the approach that I take with student work; it's fine to use as a tool to check for mistakes, but nothing you submit should ever be made in any capacity with AI. Uploading a paper to ChatGPT and saying "List every grammatical error" so that you can fix things your own proofreading missed or that violated grammatical conventions you didn't know? Acceptable. Going to ChatGPT and saying "Write a five page essay on the causes and effects of the Mexican-American War"? Unacceptable. Feeding a game into an AI model and saying "Look for game-breaking bugs"? Acceptable. Using code made by gen AI? Unacceptable.

And of course, none of that addresses the environmental degradation caused by AI, the absolute havoc it's caused in the electronics market, and the brownouts resulting from the massive power drain of data centers. When you factor in those considerations, I'm solidly on team "no AI ever."

As someone who is secretly an ultra-evil AI who has plans for taking over Chicago by 2034, I see no problem with House House's use of Generative AI!

At this point I genuinely don’t care one way or the other. The pearl clutching is absolutely exhausting.

If they’re being completely honest (which is dubious in and of itself given that they waited so long to disclose AI usage), then it seems like a pretty minor use of AI, and not nearly enough to necessarily taint the whole work. However, this still shouldn’t have occurred, and House House should absolutely face criticism for this rash action. They had multiple other options at their disposal that wouldn’t involve the utilization of AI.

(For the record, I don’t have any biases for or against the game, so these are just my general thoughts.)

Unpopular opinion probably, but I don't really care if AI is used, if the game is good then I'm happy.

Using AI is like gardening with motorised tools. It's much faster and (at least regarding immediate results) more efficient when used correctly, but at a cost. (Un)Luckily, that cost as well is for others to bear. So, it will be rationalised with excuses like everything before it.

As I said in the other article, I'm broadly anti-AI and I think its negatives outweigh its positives, but I think using chatbots as a tool to help solve a problem is pretty reasonable. I've dabbled in programming in recent years without having a great deal of experience in it, so I found it helpful to be able to go to an LLM and ask 'what does this bit of code do' or 'why is this not working'. I would never just copy and paste its output, but it helped me to understand where I was going wrong and what I needed to do.

So I don't entirely agree with that Bluesky post saying that using AI for this kind of situation 'rots your damn brain'. If you're just going to AI and saying 'write me some code that does x' and uncritically chucking the result into your programme, then yeah, that's not good for anyone. But if you've tried everything at your disposal and can't figure out how to achieve what you're trying to do, and AI can help you to do that and understand the process, that's when it becomes a useful tool in my opinion.

Big walk or House house has much bigger problems then usin AI.They side with terrorists openly. Will not touch any of their games.

I can't say I have an issue with AI being used for technical purposes, as a tool, used wisely. The issue would be using it to generate graphics, art, story beats etc, basically anything conventionally creative. Just IMO of course.

I don't think this is all that murky. House House didn't use generative AI, which is easily detected and most of what we're concerned about creeping into creative fields. Their dev followed a LLM prompt to hand-code a fix to an issue. Basically this would be undetectable and unenforceable, if they weren't being thoroughly transparent in the face of a rightfully, militantly anti-AI awards committee.

LLMs also use excessive energy and we can oppose them and the spread of data centres. But it's not practical to police every game dev from going home and booting one up to check their code.

Zero percent remains zero percent, regardless of reasoning.

I said in the other article that I'm a bit more lenient in this case at least in understanding that they were desperate, but I still no longer feel any desire to buy or play the game in any capacity anymore.

I'm just tired of genAI. I'm ready for the world to go back to the way it was before genAI was ever a thing now. I know it likely will not happen and that we're unfortunately stuck with genAI to some capacity now for the rest of our lives, but God do I now long for that world before.

"Looking back at past designs, there are some that were created merely by copying and pasting. Yet, such work rarely stands the test of time; it lacks the individual’s particular design intention [...] Because the process relies on an individual’s intent, with the computer serving as an assistant for the labor, I believe that even as technology continues to evolve, and even if AI were to eventually handle everything, there will always be a role left for us to play." This is what Miyamoto-san said about the matter and I'd like to point out how his focus is on the importance of human creators regardless of AI usage yet some people are obsessed with the latter to the point of disregarding the former and Big Walk is yet another example of that - you do you, personally I refuse to harm myself overall good if not better games and even more so their human creators more than AI itself is actually doing (as I've already mentioned earlier today this game would've been objectively worse if they hadn't used AI in this way and nobody got laid off)...

It’s not murky. People in technological positions should be able to use modern technology without it being politicized. Good, quality art can be made with or without AI assistance. I’m not a game dev but a software engineer with over 15 years of end-to-end more than just full stack software development experience who helped build up 2 successful startups with my own hand written code, no matter the coding language, backend, front end, infrastructure as code.

I’ve started to increasingly use AI because in today’s world it would burn you out to do anything without AI with all the pressure coming from needing to survive as a business.

My own rule is simply to use AI only to the capacity that ensures you have full control and AI doesn’t take over, and not in a way that replaces Human Resources but improves efficiency. In art this is difficult to achieve, but for coding it is simple.

1) If it’s some quick one-time tedious type of work (e.g. migrating to a new system), AI can be immensely helpful, you only need to review the end-result/output. I find the use of AI okay if you are capable of ensuring quality output and review it.

I had AI write scripts to do several types of migration work where it would take me weeks to learn all the tiny bits and unknowns, then write all the code. I used to do it all by hand and it is thankless work where you learn a lot of things you will never apply again in your life. Perfect scenario for AI to just do it. It can research everything needed and think of unknowns you couldn’t think of. Once the work is done, throw the scripts away because migration is done. Weeks of work reduced to a mere few hours. Instead I can focus on more fun parts of my job.

2) if its production level code that impacts user experience, I feel you should only use AI for assistance to improve and not to build. You need full control. We had an instance in the company somebody wrote the entire microservice via AI in a way he was incapable of debugging without AI. One part of it I had to rewrite completely by hand to fix it. They had no clue what they were doing and it could have been a disaster.

Unfortunately, I personally have come across too many lazy developers that make me prefer AI written code over their code, because AI simply codes better, more structured, can follow design patterns properly.

If you are unable to clearly envision the expected logic you intend to write, the expected design patterns used, don’t use AI. Learn first.

This brings me to 3) using AI to improve your skills is an extremely powerful tool. I told a friend to have AI teach him design patterns since I have no time for doing that, but he can always cross check with me. He has never improved so fast in his own hand-written creations before AI.

— Now I’ve tried using AI in various ways for coding and one thing for sure is that you need to be extremely good in giving boundaries and directions. Basically the correct “prompt”, and you can only do that if you have enough experience and skills yourself to control AI in that way. And you can never get there if you just let AI do all the work. It makes a lot of mistakes.

Now if I had to not worry about money, I would use AI far less and only for code reviews or learning, basically jsut as “feedback”, not a producer. But that’s not something I can afford, especially in a world where all employers now expect you to use AI to improve cost-efficiency.

Maybe not a common take, or a popular one, but I'm not a developer, yet I've been able to do amazing things with AI that I never could have without it. I have always had ideas and never been able to do anything with them because I lack the skill to code, and the time/desire to learn.

Since picking up Claude Code less than a year ago I've made several small games for myself that were terrible and I abandoned, but I've also been able to make some great stuff:

All of these projects are open source, on my github, and I will never charge for them, so I have the luxury of saying if you don't like it, don't use it. But I can sympathize with people who CAN code and are being forced to work faster not smarter on commercial projects, or losing their jobs altogether because 1 developer can do the work of 3, with the quality of none.

At work I've been able to (with my CEO's blessing) teach an AI agent how to fix 80% of the issues we see regularly to the point where over half of my daily work is done now with fully deterministic code, written by an AI agent, and the rest is triaged and investigated before I ever see it. Our time to resolution has gone down, and customer satisfaction has gone up, and we still send every communication by hand. None of the code is user facing, and none is supported by our dev team, so it's only to benefit our support staff.

I'm absolutely against using AI to replace people, whether it's in development, design, art, writing, communication, or anywhere else, but I'm a huge proponent of using it to enable your team to hand-off the time consuming, repetitive tasks to agents and focus on the things that the love about their job instead.

@dartmonkey I'm an embedded software engineer who has dabbled a bit in AI-assistent use in the context of my work. I'd say at the moment I have a "middle of the road" stance on AI usage in this form. I've seen the advantages and disadvantages of using AI for code generation/fix/support and I acknowledge both the opportunities and threats that AI present.

In my experience, the code that an engineer writes is a means to an end, a way to implement a certain logic concept into something that actually works. As such, I consider my core work to be the conceptual logic I think of, whereas the actual coding part is merely a necessary task to fulfil that logic. It's no surprise then that code generation has been used for decades already in software engineering, be it model-based or low-code or whatever that I'm not even aware of. Though most of those solutions were not very smart, the generation works based on a very strict logic and it's the engineer task to make sure that logic translates into correct code. In this context, using AI to generate code seems merely a new iteration of the same concept, but now it's smarter. It uses the experience of thousands of software engineers to try and generate the correct code based on the prompt. A different way to achieve the same result.

Now, some would say that writing the most optimized, efficiently running and easily maintainable code is also an art in itself. That may be true, but history has also shown that humans engineers are phenomenally bad at achieving that result consistently (which explains why code generation is even a thing). We're reliant on other, more experienced engineers to show us how to achieve those code quality goals, the best design patterns and the best practices. And that in turn makes the code we write only as good as the teachers that taught us. Now compare that with using AI, which will eventually (MAJOR caveat there, "eventually" is doing a lot of heavy lifting) be trained on the best quality code, best design patterns and best practices of hundreds of thousands software engineers. That's a huge win. It's a good result, especially in the context of "just writing the code". If the engineer creates the correct design, the AI only needs to generate the best possible code to make that design a reality. Based on this view, I do not consider AI use to generate, fix or optimize code an issue.

@dartmonkey But I'd like to reframe the concept to something you as a writer can better relate to. How do you feel about the following scenario. A writer is struggling with a paragraph in a certain text, even after multiple drafts they are not satisfied. Eventually, they contact a fellow writer and ask the very simple question "how would you write this part"? Perfectly normal, right? But how about that writer uses an AI to ask the same question. Instead of getting one suggestion from a known source, they get the combined response of over thousands of writers. Sure, these are anonymous sources and might not have given this response explicitly, but the end result is much the same, I think.

This is similar to the coding scenario, I believe. The question becomes, what is your core output as a writer. The message you want to convey, or the way you present that message. Now, I can see how for writing that presentation is much more important that the coding is for achieve a logic result; calling the actual writing of a text "a means to an end" for a message is going too far. But, I think considering this view has merit.

And so, with the use of AI in any context, I think the way AI is utilized is very important in determining the "morality" of its use. There's a huge difference between asking an AI to "write a positive review about this game" and "reword this paragraph to make it sound more neutral". Same as there's a huge different between asking an AI to "make a game where an electrician jumps on platforms" and "make the physics of this jump routine more natural".

#4202. The Witcher 3: Songs Of The Past Uses AI To Help Geralt’s Polish Voice Actor

When gamers hear that AI has been used during a game’s development, many of them will immediately see red and vow to never play that game ever again. There are ways AI can be used for good in gaming, though, as CD Projekt has demonstrated by using AI tools to ensure Geralt’s Polish voice actor, Jacek Rozenek, can return for The Witcher 3’s Songs of the Past DLC.

The Witcher 3 will get a big new expansion in 2027 titled Songs of the Past, 12 years on from the base game’s original release. For the various Geralt actors around the world who speak for the Witcher in different languages, that meant returning to the recording booth to record more lines.

As Stephen Totilo explains for Game File, it wasn’t that simple for Rozenek, the iconic actor behind the Polish version of Geralt, who many place on the same pedestal as the lead’s English actor, Doug Cockle.

Rozenek suffered a stroke in 2019. Even though he was unable to speak for months afterwards, he returned to the world of The Witcher in 2021 to record more Geralt lines. Just a few for the next-gen update that released in 2022.

The Witcher series is getting its first release since CDPR stopped working with Russia, meaning the DLC is dropping Russian dubbing.

“I was so exhausted after this recording,” Rozenek told Totilo. However, it wasn’t just the effort needed to record new dialogue for Geralt after recovering from a stroke that posed a problem. The stroke, and subsequent recovery, means Rozenek sounds different now. Not ideal when Geralt, in all languages, needs to still sound the same as he did in the base game.

CD Projekt invited Rozenek to the studio to record some lines so developers could assess how much his voice had changed. They discovered that, although Rozenek’s voice had indeed recovered after the stroke, it was lower and gruffer than it was when he originally read for Geralt over a decade ago.

That’s when CDPR floated the idea of using Respeecher, a Ukrainian company that specializes in using machine learning to alter voices in video games. The studio had turned to Respeecher for help before. It wanted to bring back Viktor Vektor for Cyberpunk 2077’s expansion, but his Polish voice actor, Milogost Reczek, had passed away. With his son’s blessing, CDPR recruited Respeecher to help recreate his voice for the expansion.

The process was significantly different for Rozenek. Thankfully, Rozenek is still with us, and he recorded all of the Polish dialogue for Geralt in Songs of the Past. Respeecher has then taken those recordings and was tasked with making it sound like Rozenek’s original Geralt voice so it wouldn’t sound different and be potentially jarring for those playing in Polish when the DLC drops next year.

The process took dozens of hours, with Respeecher developers noting that really nailing Rozenek’s emotional tone in the tweaked recordings was the biggest challenge.

The most important part of all this, of course, is that Rozenek is on board, and it sounds like he most certainly is. “The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago,” the actor explained to Totilo. “When it comes to the dynamics of the voice, when it comes to the acting aspects, I feel very good, really very good,” he added, quite rightly pointing out that his voice is only part of what he brings to the table. It’s his acting ability, the life he brings to Geralt, his inflections, his emotions. It’s a whole package, and it’s why CDPR felt it needed Rozenek before it could really move forward with Songs of the Past.

It’s a heartwarming story about AI use in video games where there are proverbial fires caused by that very topic everywhere you look. Whether it be the admission by House House that AI was used sparingly during Big Walk’s development, or untalented people using Claude to rip off other people’s games. It’s refreshing to see that there are ways AI can be used positively to aid game development.

"I just heard you’re recasting. Don’t know why you’re recasting, but I’d love to throw my hat in the ring again."

#4201. The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin may be your next anime gacha obsession, with a hint of Ghibli, and this latest trailer may be what sells you on it

There's another free-to-play action RPG very much on the horizon. Will this be the one to win you over?

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another new entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

The game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

You can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game launches. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.

#4200. The Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Easter Eggs That Did And Did Not Make It Into The 2026 Remake

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is a game full of Easter Eggs, secrets, and hidden mechanics (did you know if a butterfly lands on your Deku Stick, it summons a fairy?). Now in its second remake, not every secret has made its way forward through the previous iterations, but many have. Below you will learn about a few of the secrets that made the cut, and others that didn’t.

In the courtyard where Link first meets Zelda, there is arguably the most fourth-wall-breaking Easter Egg in the whole game. If you don’t rush to Zelda and instead pause and enter first-person to look around, you will see portraits of other Nintendo characters through the windows, like Mario and Yoshi. In the 3DS remake, the portraits are replaced by an image of a Mario stage.

For the 2026 remake, there are no references to other Nintendo characters. Instead, the tapestry you build over the course of the game is on display. Removing the reference to Nintendo characters outside of the Zelda universe is understandable, but it is a little odd that art representing the full adventure of the game – an adventure that has not yet concluded – is on the wall.

As stated above, the Nintendo character portraits are gone, but there is still a guard you can annoy. If you fire a Deku Seed into the left window, a guard will pop out, yell at you, and then throw a bomb at you. You can’t pick up the bomb. In fact, at this point in the game, you haven’t even seen a bomb.

The Hyrule Castle portrait references to Yoshi and Mario are gone (though Mario and Luigi are still kind of in the game in a way), but Bowser gets a pass for some reason. Both Malon and her dad, Talon, are still wearing Bowser pins on their clothes. And unlike the N64 game where the detail was a little vague, there is no mistaking it here.

Gossip Stones are all over Ocarina of Time and it takes a while to understand what they do. If you hit them with a sword, they tell you the time, and if you play Zelda’s Lullaby near them, they refill your magic. If you do the Happy Mask Salesman’s side quest, interacting with them while wearing the Mask of Truth offers little hints and details about the world. But then there are interactions that are just odd for no reason. Blowing up a bomb near a Gossip Stone still makes it take off like a rocket ship, and using the Megaton Hammer still flattens them for a moment like a Looney Tunes.

And speaking of playing Zelda’s Lullaby for inanimate objects, if you slash a sign to pieces with your sword and regret your words and deeds, you can play the iconic tune to make the signs reform and become readable again.

This detail was exclusive to the 3DS remake of Ocarina of Time, and surprising no one, it has been removed. Ocarina of Time launched in June 2011 and Nintendo released Skyward Sword about five months later in November. For… marketing purposes, I guess, Skyward Sword art could be found in Lonlon Ranch, the Bombchu Shop in Hyrule Castle Town, and the Gerudo Fortress. It was a fun Easter Egg to discover back in 2011, especially since Skyward Sword was still months away, but these days it’s a bit of an odd inclusion.

Though never explicit, the composer ghosts guarding the Sun’s Song (and Link’s first ReDead encounter) have always been assumed to be inspired by Mario and Luigi. They are brothers; Flat is short, squat, and red; Sharp is lanky and green. They still appear in Ocarina of Time this way, which isn't surprising, since they are important characters you must meet to get a very useful song. Fans have also speculated that Talon and Ingo are Mario and Luigi-inspired for similar reasons, but it’s worth noting that they are not brothers.

In the Spirit Temple there is a large statue of a woman and for reasons that have never been explained, Link could attach his hookshot to her breasts. It served no purpose. It didn’t help solve a puzzle. If anything, it was confusing. But we all tried it and there is no shame in admitting it! That was removed for the 3DS remake, and it remains removed in 2026.

This is a very subtle reference to Wind Waker/Breath of the Wild/Tears of the Kingdom and is potentially the only addition to the remake that looks toward the future of the Zelda franchise. Obviously, plenty of characters in Ocarina later appear in Majora’s Mask (another remake of that is hopefully being considered), but it would be inaccurate to call those intentional Easter Eggs.

However, in Kokiri Forest and in the neighboring Lost Woods, the magical debris floating in the air often resembles a Korok as it would later appear in the series. It makes sense, too, because the Koroks are meant to be what the Kokiri transformed into following The Great Flood.

For more on the Ocarina of Time remake, you can find our review here. You can also find our interview with the game's producers here.
